ap_physics_1-m01.stem: A solid sphere and a solid disk, each of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and radius $0.2\text{ m}$, are mounted on identical frictionless axles through their centers and start from rest. The same constant torque of $2\text{ N m}$ is applied to each for $6\text{ s}$. Which statement about the angular speeds after $6\text{ s}$ is correct and best justified?

options.text: The solid sphere is spinning faster ($187\text{ rad/s}$ compared with $150\text{ rad/s}$), because the same torque gives a larger angular acceleration to the object with the smaller rotational inertia.
options.why: The angular acceleration is $\alpha=\tau/I$ with $I=0.0640\text{ kg m}^2$ for the solid sphere and $0.0800\text{ kg m}^2$ for the solid disk, so $\omega=\alpha t$ is larger for the solid sphere.

options.text: The solid disk is spinning faster, because it has the larger rotational inertia and so it stores more rotational energy.
options.why: Confuses a larger rotational inertia with a larger angular speed; the same torque gives it a smaller angular acceleration.

options.text: The solid sphere is spinning faster, because the torque acts for a longer time on it.
options.why: Invents a different time of action; the torque acts on both objects for the same time.

options.text: The two objects are spinning at the same speed, because they have the same mass, the same radius and the same torque.
options.why: Overlooks that the rotational inertia also depends on how the mass is distributed.
